title: CI/CD Pipelines
tagline: Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment — automated pipelines that build, test, and ship software on every commit.

sections.content:
**CI/CD** transforms software delivery from a manual, error-prone process into an automated assembly line. **Continuous Integration (CI)** means every developer's code change is automatically built and tested the moment it is pushed — catching bugs within minutes rather than days. **Continuous Delivery (CD)** extends this by always keeping the codebase in a deployable state, ready to ship to production on demand. **Continuous Deployment** goes one step further: every green build is automatically deployed to production with no human approval gate.

Together, these practices eliminate 'integration hell', reduce the batch size of each release, and let teams get feedback from real users faster. The pipeline is the backbone: a series of automated stages — build, test, package, deploy — that each commit must pass in sequence.

sections.title: The Automated Baggage Conveyor
sections.content:
Imagine an airport baggage system. Without CI/CD, every bag (code change) is carried by hand from check-in to the plane — slow, inconsistent, and prone to being lost or mixed up. **CI** is the automated conveyor belt: every bag is placed on it immediately and automatically scanned for prohibited items (linting), weighed (build check), and X-rayed (tests). Only bags that pass all checks continue.

**Continuous Delivery** means the bags always arrive at the gate ready to board — the decision to load them onto the plane is made by a human (a manual deploy button). **Continuous Deployment** removes even that final step: passing bags are automatically loaded. The conveyor never stops, the process is consistent, and problems are caught at the scanner — not on the tarmac. **Artifacts** (the packaged build output — a Docker image, a zip file, a compiled binary) are the labeled bags: created once, tagged with a version, and shipped to each destination rather than rebuilt from scratch at every stop.

A CI/CD **pipeline** is a sequence of stages executed automatically when code is pushed. The most common stages are:

**1. Source** — The pipeline is triggered by a Git event: a push to a branch, a pull request opening, or a merge to `main`. The CI system checks out the exact commit.

**2. Build** — Compile source code, run a linter and type-checker. The goal is to confirm the code is syntactically valid and conforms to style rules. Fast feedback — often under 60 seconds.

**3. Test** — Run unit tests (fast, isolated) then integration tests (slower, real I/O). If any test fails the pipeline stops and notifies the author. This is the most important gate.

**4. Package / Artifact** — A successful test stage produces an **artifact**: an immutable, versioned build output. In a containerised system this is a Docker image pushed to a registry. In a Node.js service it might be a tarball. The artifact is built *once* and promoted through environments — never rebuilt from source again.

**5. Deploy to Staging** — The artifact is deployed to a staging environment that mirrors production. Smoke tests and E2E tests run here.

**6. Deploy to Production** — In Continuous Delivery a human clicks 'approve'. In Continuous Deployment this step is automatic. Both approaches rely on fast rollback capability if issues appear post-deploy.

**GitHub Actions** is the most widely used CI/CD platform for open-source and many enterprise projects. A workflow is defined in a YAML file at `.github/workflows/`. Each workflow has `on:` triggers, `jobs:`, and `steps:`. Steps run `run:` shell commands or `uses:` community actions (pre-built steps for checkout, Node.js setup, Docker login, etc.).

sections.caption: GitHub Actions workflow structure: jobs run on virtual machines, steps compose reusable actions and shell commands.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.code:
# .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  ci:
    name: Build & Test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Lint
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Type check
        run: npm run type-check

      - name: Unit tests
        run: npm test -- --coverage --ci

      - name: Upload coverage report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage-report
          path: coverage/

  build-and-push:
    name: Build Docker Image
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: ci
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Log in to container registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          push: true
          # Tag with git SHA for immutable artifact traceability
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}

  deploy-production:
    name: Deploy to Production
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: build-and-push
    environment: production   # requires manual approval in GitHub

    steps:
      - name: Deploy via SSH
        run: |
          ssh deploy@${{ secrets.PROD_HOST }} \
            "docker pull ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }} && \
             docker compose up -d"
sections.explanation: The workflow has three jobs that chain via `needs:`. The `ci` job runs on every push and PR. `build-and-push` only runs on `main` after CI passes — it produces a Docker image tagged with the exact git SHA (the artifact). `deploy-production` uses a GitHub Environment with a required reviewer, giving one-click human approval before the image goes live. This is Continuous Delivery: always ready, human-gated final step.

sections.label: Concept
sections.code:
# ── Key CI/CD concepts ──────────────────────────────────────────

# 1. ARTIFACT IMMUTABILITY
# Build once, promote the same artifact through environments.
# Never rebuild from source for staging vs production.
# Tag with git SHA or semantic version:
#   my-service:1.4.2
#   my-service:abc1234   (git SHA)

# 2. ENVIRONMENT PROMOTION
#   commit --> CI (unit tests)
#              --> staging (integration + smoke)
#                          --> production (same artifact, different config)

# 3. SECRETS MANAGEMENT
# Never hard-code secrets in workflow files.
# Use GitHub Secrets (Settings > Secrets):
#   ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}
#   ${{ secrets.DOCKER_TOKEN }}

# 4. MATRIX BUILDS — test across multiple versions in parallel
# jobs:
#   test:
#     strategy:
#       matrix:
#         node-version: [18, 20, 22]
#     steps:
#       - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
#         with:
#           node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}

# 5. PIPELINE SPEED TIPS
#   - Cache node_modules between runs (actions/cache or cache: npm)
#   - Run lint + unit tests in parallel jobs
#   - Only run E2E tests on the main branch, not every PR
#   - Use --ci flag in Jest: no interactive mode, fail on coverage drop

# 6. CONTINUOUS INTEGRATION vs DELIVERY vs DEPLOYMENT
#   CI         = auto build + test on every push
#   CD Deliver = CI + always deployable + HUMAN approves production push
#   CD Deploy  = CI + auto deploy to production on every green build

echo "Pipeline philosophy: small batches, fast feedback, always green main"

sections.content: **Keep the main branch always green.** The golden rule of CI/CD is that `main` (or `master`) must always be in a deployable state. Enforce this with branch protection rules: require the CI workflow to pass before a PR can merge, and require at least one reviewer approval. If a bad commit slips through, roll it back immediately rather than piling on fixes — a broken `main` blocks every other developer on the team.

items: **CI (Continuous Integration)** automatically builds and tests every code change on push, catching integration bugs within minutes rather than days.
**Continuous Delivery** keeps the codebase always deployable, with a manual approval gate before production; **Continuous Deployment** removes that gate entirely.
**Pipeline stages** (build → lint → test → package → deploy) form a sequential quality gate — each stage must pass before the next begins.
**Artifacts** are built once, tagged immutably (git SHA or semver), and promoted through environments — never rebuilt from source per environment.
**GitHub Actions** workflows are YAML files in `.github/workflows/`; jobs can run in parallel or chain with `needs:`, and secrets keep credentials out of code.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
options: Continuous Delivery runs tests automatically; Continuous Deployment does not.
Continuous Delivery requires a manual approval before deploying to production; Continuous Deployment deploys automatically on every green build.
Continuous Deployment only works with containerised applications.
Continuous Delivery skips staging environments to ship faster.
quiz.explanation: Continuous Delivery means every green build is *ready* to deploy, but a human chooses when to push the button. Continuous Deployment removes that human gate — every passing build goes live automatically.

quiz.question: Why should a Docker image be tagged with the git commit SHA?
options: It makes the image smaller by compressing layers.
It allows the CI system to skip rebuilding unchanged layers.
It creates an immutable link between the running artifact and the exact source code it was built from.
It is required by Docker Hub's terms of service.
quiz.explanation: Tagging with the git SHA makes the artifact immutable and traceable. You can always determine which code version is running in production, and roll back by redeploying an older SHA image.

quiz.question: In a GitHub Actions workflow, what does `needs: ci` on a job mean?
options: The job requires Node.js CI mode to be enabled.
The job will only run if the `ci` job completed successfully.
The job shares the same runner as the `ci` job.
The job downloads artifacts from the `ci` job automatically.
quiz.explanation: `needs:` defines job dependencies. A job with `needs: ci` will not start until the `ci` job finishes successfully. If `ci` fails, the dependent job is skipped, preventing a broken build from reaching deploy stages.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of `npm ci` over `npm install` in a CI pipeline?
options: It installs packages faster by skipping post-install scripts.
It installs only production dependencies, ignoring devDependencies.
It performs a clean install strictly from package-lock.json, failing if there are any discrepancies — ensuring reproducible builds.
It automatically upgrades all packages to their latest versions.
quiz.explanation: `npm ci` deletes `node_modules`, then installs exactly the versions in `package-lock.json`. It fails if lock file and `package.json` are out of sync. This guarantees every CI run uses the same dependency tree.

quiz.question: A matrix build strategy in GitHub Actions is primarily used to:
options: Run tests on multiple Node.js versions, operating systems, or configurations in parallel.
Deploy to multiple production regions simultaneously.
Split a single large test suite into smaller parallel chunks.
Build both a staging and production Docker image from one job.
quiz.explanation: Matrix builds fan out a job across a set of parameter combinations (e.g., Node 18/20/22 × ubuntu/windows). Each combination runs as a separate parallel job, ensuring compatibility across environments.

quiz.question: Which pipeline stage produces the artifact?
options: The source checkout stage.
The linting stage.
The package or build stage, after tests pass.
The deploy-to-staging stage.
quiz.explanation: The artifact (Docker image, tarball, binary) is created only after tests pass. Producing it earlier would waste compute on code that is known to be broken. The artifact is then promoted through environments.

quiz.question: Why should secrets never be hard-coded in a workflow YAML file?
options: YAML files do not support string values longer than 64 characters.
GitHub Actions cannot read YAML comments, so secrets would be ignored.
Workflow files are committed to source control, making hard-coded secrets visible to anyone with repository access.
Hard-coded secrets cause pipeline timeouts on large repositories.
quiz.explanation: Workflow files live in the repository and are visible to contributors. Hard-coded credentials become public (or at least accessible to all repo members). GitHub Secrets stores values encrypted, injecting them only at runtime.

quiz.question: What does it mean for the `main` branch to be 'always green'?
options: The branch is protected with a green-colored badge in the GitHub UI.
Every commit on `main` has passed all automated tests and the codebase is in a deployable state at all times.
Only senior developers with 'green' access can merge into `main`.
The branch automatically deploys to production after each merge.
quiz.explanation: An always-green `main` means CI enforces that no broken code can merge. Branch protection rules require status checks to pass before a PR merges, so you can deploy from `main` at any moment with confidence.

quiz.question: In the pipeline stage order, why does the 'deploy to production' stage come after 'deploy to staging'?
options: Production servers are geographically closer, so the staging deploy warms the CDN cache first.
Staging allows running smoke and integration tests against the real artifact in a production-like environment before risking real user traffic.
It is a GitHub Actions limitation: environments must be deployed alphabetically.
Staging deployment compresses the Docker image to reduce production bandwidth.
quiz.explanation: Staging mirrors production configuration. Deploying there first lets you run smoke tests and integration checks on the real artifact. Only after those pass does the same artifact proceed to production, minimising the risk of regressions reaching users.

quiz.question: A team's CI pipeline takes 45 minutes to run. What is the most effective first step to reduce this?
options: Switch from YAML to JSON workflow definitions.
Remove all E2E tests from the pipeline entirely.
Cache dependencies between runs and run lint, unit tests, and type-checking as parallel jobs.
Reduce the number of branches developers are allowed to create.
quiz.explanation: Dependency installation and independent tasks are the biggest time sinks. Caching `node_modules` eliminates repeated installs. Running lint, type-check, and unit tests as parallel jobs can cut wall-clock time dramatically without removing any quality gates.
